Learn what JSON translation files are, how the t() function works, why developers use en.json and fr.json, and how to organize multilingual applications the right way. 6 min read Just now -- Press enter or click to view image in full size You’re building a new feature and come across this line t("welcome")Or maybe you notice files like en.json, fr.json, or de.json in your project. At first, they look like ordinary JSON files. But they’re actually one of the most important parts of software localization. If you’ve ever wondered what these JSON translation files are, why developers use them, or how they help applications support multiple languages, you’re in the right place. In this guide, we’ll understand JSON translation files, how they work, why they’re important for multilingual applications, and the best practices every developer should know. Before We Begin: What is JSON? Before talking about translation files, let’s quickly understand what JSON actually is. JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation. Despite the name, it isn’t only used with JavaScript. It’s simply a lightweight format for storing data that both humans and computers can read easily. Here’s a simple example: { "name": "John", "role": "Developer", "country": "India" }Everything is stored as a key-value pair. • name is the key. • "John" is the value. JSON is used almost everywhere — APIs, configuration files, databases, and localization. Its simple structure is one of the reasons developers love working with it. What Are JSON Translation Files? A JSON translation file is a file that stores all the text used in your application for a specific language. Instead of writing text directly inside your code, you store it in a JSON file and let your application load the correct language automatically. Think of it like a dictionary. Whenever your application needs to display text, it simply looks up the correct translation instead of storing the words inside the component. For example: { "welcome": "Welcome", "login": "Login", "logout": "Logout", "profile": "Profile" }Here: • welcome, login, logout, and profile are translation keys • The values are the actual text users see. Why Use JSON Instead of Hardcoding Text? When you’re building a small project, writing text directly inside your components feels completely normal.

Welcome

It works perfectly… Until someone asks: “Can I use your app in French?” Then another user requests German. Another wants Japanese. Suddenly every heading, button, notification, and error message needs to be translated. Imagine updating hundreds of files every time you add a new language. That’s not practical. Instead, developers write something like this:

{t("welcome")}

Now your application doesn’t care which language the user speaks. It simply asks for the value of the welcome key. The translation file does the rest. What Does t() Actually Do? If you’re new to localization, you’ve probably wondered what this function does. t("welcome")The t() function stands for translation. It doesn’t translate anything by itself. Instead, it searches for the welcome key inside the currently selected language file. If the user’s language is English, it reads: en.jsonIf the user switches to French, it reads: fr.jsonThe key stays exactly the same. Only the value changes. That’s why developers don’t need separate code for every language. Supporting Multiple Languages Let’s say your application supports English, French, and German. English (en.json) { "welcome": "Welcome", "login": "Login", "logout": "Logout" }French (fr.json) { "welcome": "Bienvenue", "login": "Connexion", "logout": "Déconnexion" }German (de.json) { "welcome": "Willkommen", "login": "Anmelden", "logout": "Abmelden" }Notice something important. The keys never change. Only the translated values change. When a user switches languages, your application simply loads a different JSON file. The code stays exactly the same. A Real-World Example Imagine you’re building an e-commerce website. Your product page has an Add to Cart button. Instead of writing: you write: Now your translation files look like this. English { "cart.add": "Add to Cart" }French { "cart.add": "Ajouter au panier" }Japanese { "cart.add": "カートに追加" }The button component never changes. Only the translation file changes. Whether your application supports two languages or twenty, the same code continues to work. That’s one of the biggest reasons developers use JSON translation files. Why Developers Prefer JSON Translation Files JSON translation files make localization much easier because they: • Keep all translations organized in one place • Make adding new languages simple • Separate content from application code • Allow translators to work without touching the codebase • Reduce duplicate text across the application • Make projects easier to maintain as they grow This is why frameworks like React, Next.js, Vue, Angular, React Native, and many localization libraries rely on JSON translation files. Organizing Translation Files As your application grows, keeping everything inside one file becomes difficult. Most projects organize translations like this: locales/ │ ├── en/ │ ├── common.json │ ├── auth.json │ └── dashboard.json │ ├── fr/ │ ├── common.json │ ├── auth.json │ └── dashboard.json │ └── de/ ├── common.json ├── auth.json └── dashboard.jsonInstead of one massive file, translations are grouped by features. This makes them much easier to manage as the project grows. Using Better Translation Keys Another common mistake is using unclear translation keys. For example: { "text1": "Login", "button2": "Logout", "abc": "Profile" }After a few months, nobody remembers what those keys mean. A better approach is using meaningful names. { "auth.login": "Login", "auth.logout": "Logout", "profile.title": "Profile", "cart.add": "Add to Cart" }Good translation keys make projects much easier to understand and maintain. Common Mistakes Developers Make When developers start working with localization, they often make the same mistakes. Hardcoding text inside components Using confusing translation keys Forgetting to update every language after adding a new feature Keeping thousands of translations inside one huge JSON file Using different key names across different languages A little planning in the beginning can save hours of work later. As Your Project Grows… Managing one language is easy. Managing ten languages isn’t. Every new feature means adding new translation keys, checking missing translations, reviewing updates, and keeping every language synchronized. Doing all of this manually quickly becomes repetitive and error-prone. This is where localization platforms become useful. Platforms like Babelize automatically detect new content, manage JSON translation files, keep multiple languages synchronized, and reduce repetitive manual work. Instead of spending time maintaining translation files, developers can focus on building better products. Frequently Asked Questions What is a JSON translation file? A JSON translation file stores translated text for a specific language, allowing an application to display content based on the user’s selected language. Are JSON translation files only used in React? No. They’re commonly used with React, Next.js, Vue, Angular, React Native, and many other modern frameworks. What is a translation key? A translation key is a unique identifier like welcome or cart.add that points to translated text inside a language file. Why use JSON instead of hardcoding text? JSON keeps translations separate from your code, making applications easier to maintain, update, and scale as more languages are added. What’s the difference between i18n and localization? Internationalization (i18n) is the process of designing an application so it can support multiple languages and regions. Localization (l10n) is the process of adapting that application for a specific language or region using translation files, localized dates, currencies, and more. Final Thoughts JSON translation files may look simple, but they’re one of the building blocks of modern localization. They help developers separate text from code, organize translations, and make applications ready for users around the world. Whether you’re building a React application, a SaaS platform, a mobile app, or an AI product, understanding how JSON translation files work is an important step toward creating a great multilingual experience. As your project grows, keeping translations organized becomes just as important as writing good code. Starting with a clean translation structure today will save you countless hours in the future. If you’re already learning about localization, you may also want to explore how localization goes beyond translation and adapts the entire user experience for different languages and regions.
